steps: Clip the safety cord, which is the small red cord on the treadmill, to your clothing, before starting. If you trip, it pulls out and stops the belt.
Start the treadmill at a slow walk and let it warm you up for a few minutes.
Increase the speed gradually until you're running at a pace you can keep up. Aim for a pace where you could still say a short sentence.
Stand tall with your chest up, your arms bent at about a right angle, and your shoulders relaxed. Look straight ahead, not down at your feet.
When you're finished, slow to a walk for a few minutes to let your heart rate come down before you stop.
watchFor: Keep off the handrails while you run. Only hold them to steady yourself when starting or stopping.
Land softly and don't take huge strides. If you feel pain in your knees or shins, slow down or stop.
Step off only when the belt has fully stopped.

steps: Clip the safety cord, the small red cord on the treadmill, to your clothing before starting.
Start the treadmill at a slow speed and step onto the belt with both feet.
Increase the speed until you're walking briskly. Your breathing should be quicker, but you should still be able to talk.
Stand tall with your chest up, your shoulders relaxed, and your arms swinging naturally. Look straight ahead.
Walk for the time you've set. To finish, slow down for a couple of minutes before stopping.
watchFor: Don't hold the handrails for the whole walk. That changes how you move and takes away some of the effort.
Don't look down at your feet, which strains your neck and throws off your balance.
Step off only when the belt has fully stopped.

steps: Wear shoes made for running, and comfortable clothing suited to the weather. Choose a route without heavy traffic, ideally a park, track, or sidewalk.
Start with a few minutes of walking to warm up, then ease into a slow jog.
Run at a pace where you could still say a short sentence. If you can't, slow down.
Stand tall with your chest up, your shoulders relaxed, and your arms bent at about a right angle. Land softly.
When you're finished, walk for a few minutes to let your heart rate come down.
watchFor: Stay aware of traffic and your surroundings. If you wear headphones, keep the volume low enough to hear what's around you.
Bring water for longer runs, and let someone know your route.
Slow down or stop if you feel pain in your knees, shins, or feet. Don't push through sharp pain.

steps: Adjust the seat so that when your foot is at the lowest point of the pedal, your knee is slightly bent, not fully straight. Adjust the handlebars so you sit comfortably.
Put your feet on the pedals and secure the straps if there are any. Start pedaling slowly to warm up.
Increase the resistance and speed to a level where you're working but can still say a short sentence.
Sit up tall with a relaxed grip on the handlebars and your shoulders down away from your ears. Keep your knees pointing straight ahead.
When you're finished, pedal slowly for a few minutes to cool down.
watchFor: If your knees hurt, check the seat height. A seat that's too low is a common cause.
Don't grip the handlebars tightly or hunch your shoulders.
Wait until the pedals have fully stopped before you get off.

steps: Step onto the machine and hold the handles. Place your feet flat on the pedals.
Start moving your legs in a smooth, oval motion, like you're walking or running without hitting the ground.
Let your arms move with the handles, pushing and pulling. Or hold the fixed handles if that feels better.
Adjust the resistance so you're working but can still say a short sentence.
Stand tall with your chest up and your eyes forward. When you're finished, slow down for a couple of minutes before stepping off.
watchFor: Keep your feet flat on the pedals, and don't lift your heels.
Don't lean heavily on the handles. Stand upright.
Wait until the pedals have stopped before getting off.

steps: Step onto the machine and hold the side rails lightly. Start at a slow speed so you can get used to the rhythm.
Step up one stair at a time, placing your whole foot on each step. Keep your knees pointing forward.
Increase the speed slowly until you're working hard but can still say a short sentence.
Stand tall, with your chest up and your eyes forward. Let your arms swing naturally, or rest your fingers lightly on the rails.
When you're finished, slow the speed down for a couple of minutes and then step off.
watchFor: Don't lean on the rails or hunch over, which reduces the workout and strains your back.
Place your whole foot on each step, not just your toes.
If you feel dizzy or your knees hurt, slow down or stop.

steps: Sit on the seat with your feet strapped into the footplates, and hold the handle with both hands. Start with your knees bent, arms straight, and leaning slightly forward.
Push with your legs first, driving the seat back.
As your legs straighten, lean back slightly, then pull the handle toward your lower ribs with your elbows going back.
To come back, do it in reverse: straighten your arms first, lean forward, then bend your knees to slide the seat forward.
Keep a smooth, steady rhythm, with the effort at the push. Set a pace you can keep for the time you've set.
watchFor: The order matters: legs, then body, then arms on the way back, and arms, body, then legs on the way forward.
Keep your back flat and don't round your shoulders forward or lean back too far.
Don't yank the handle. Use a smooth pull.

steps: Choose a rope that reaches your armpits when you stand on the middle of it. Wear supportive shoes and use a flat, smooth surface with some space around you.
Hold a handle in each hand with your elbows close to your sides, and swing the rope over your head using your wrists, not your whole arms.
Jump just a small hop off the floor, just high enough for the rope to pass under your feet.
Land softly on the balls of your feet, with your knees slightly bent.
Keep a steady rhythm. When you're tired, rest and start again.
watchFor: Keep your jumps small. Jumping high wastes energy and puts more stress on your ankles and knees.
Don't jump on a hard surface like concrete if you can avoid it.
If you trip on the rope, just stop, reset, and start again.

steps: Swim in a pool with a lifeguard on duty, or in a place where you know it's safe to swim. Start with an easy warm-up length.
Choose a stroke you're comfortable with. Keep your body flat and long in the water, and kick from your hips.
Breathe out steadily into the water and turn your head to breathe in, rather than holding your breath.
Swim at a pace you can keep for the time you've set, resting at the wall when you need to.
Finish with a few slow, easy lengths to cool down.
watchFor: Never swim alone. If you're not a confident swimmer, stay in shallow water or ask for lessons.
Take a break if you feel tired or cramped, and stay near the wall.
Don't swim right after a large meal, and drink water. You can get dehydrated even in the pool.

steps: Wear a helmet that fits snugly, and check that your tires have air and your brakes work. Choose a route that suits your comfort, ideally with bike paths or quiet roads.
Adjust your seat so that your knee is slightly bent when your foot is at the lowest point of the pedal.
Start pedaling slowly to warm up, then build to a steady pace where you could still say a short sentence.
Sit up tall with a relaxed grip and your shoulders down. Keep your eyes up and look ahead.
Cool down with a few minutes of easy pedaling at the end.
watchFor: Always wear a helmet, and follow traffic rules. Use hand signals and stay visible with lights or bright clothing.
Bring water for longer rides.
If you feel pain in your knees, check your seat height and slow down.

steps: Wear comfortable shoes with good grip, dress for the weather, and bring water and a snack. Choose a trail that matches your fitness, and tell someone where you're going.
Start at an easy pace to warm up. Walk at a steady speed where you can talk in short sentences.
On uphills, take shorter steps and lean into the slope slightly. On downhills, take small steps and keep your knees slightly bent.
Watch where you place your feet, especially on loose rocks, roots, or wet ground.
Take breaks to drink water and rest as you need.
watchFor: Stay on marked trails, and turn around if the weather turns bad or you're getting tired.
Bring a phone and a small first-aid kit, and make sure you have enough water and time before dark.
Take small steps on steep downhills to protect your knees.
